steps.prompt: What decides whether you use to + verb or verb + -ing?
options: The first verb — each verb takes one pattern.
Whether the sentence is positive or negative.
steps.answer: The first verb — each verb takes one pattern.
steps.why: There is no rule of meaning. Decide takes to; enjoy takes -ing. You learn them with the verb.

steps.title: Which pattern does the verb take?
steps.html:
verb + to + base formverb + -ing
decide to change careerenjoy working at the weekend
want to have childrenstop thinking about it
hope to pass the examskeep working four days a week
plan to retire in Junedon’t mind starting late
learn to swimfinish studying
need / would like to talkgive up / can’t stand waiting

+ to: decide, want, hope, plan, need, learn, would like, expect, promise, choose, offer, agree.

+ -ing: enjoy, stop, keep, finish, give up, don’t mind, can’t stand, regret, take up, look forward to.

A few verbs take both with almost the same meaning: start, begin, continue, like, love, hate. He began studying law = He began to study law.

After a preposition, always use -ing: She is interested in working abroad. He is tired of waiting.

You met the -ing form after like / love / can’t stand in Lesson 3. It comes back as a full topic in Unit 10.

steps.title: Three people who started again
steps.html:
Most people decide on a career in their twenties and stop thinking about it. These three did the opposite.

Nadia was a lawyer for eleven years. She was good at it, but she hated going to the office. At thirty-four she left home for the first time in her life, moved to another city and started training to become a nurse. “I didn’t want to spend another decade doing something I disliked,” she says. She finished her training in her late thirties and now works nights in a children’s hospital. She has never regretted leaving law.

Tomas took up the guitar when he was a teenager. He kept playing all through university, but he chose to study engineering because it seemed safer. He worked as an engineer until he was forty-two. Then his company closed. Instead of looking for another job, he decided to teach music. He now performs in a small concert hall twice a month and enjoys teaching more than he expected.

Grace is the oldest of the three. She retired at sixty-one and immediately got bored. She avoided telling her family, but she missed working. So, in her sixties, she began studying again — and last year she qualified as a conductor. She hopes to lead a full orchestra before she is seventy.

None of them planned to change direction. All three would do it again.

Their advice is similar. Expect to feel foolish for about a year. Avoid asking people who have never changed anything. And do not give up doing something you love just because somebody tells you it is not a real job.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text. Nadia, Tomas and Grace are invented, and no words are attributed to a real person.
